findings.body:
`NewClient()` sets `InsecureSkipVerify: true` for every caller, with no environment or build-time gate. Any attacker who can intercept ledger traffic can present an arbitrary certificate and MITM requests — reading or altering ledger payloads in staging and production alike. The comment names staging and TICKET-77, but this constructor has no env/config argument, so production inherits skip-verify as soon as this ships.

Pin the staging CA with `tls.Config.RootCAs` (or a pinned leaf), or gate skip-verify behind an explicit non-production flag that defaults to verifying.

summary:
Looks good is the wrong verdict — this change disables TLS certificate verification for every ledger HTTP call, with no environment gate.

`NewClient()` now installs a custom `http.Transport` whose `tls.Config` sets `InsecureSkipVerify: true`. The comment frames this as a staging workaround (TICKET-77), but the constructor takes no env, config, or build tag: production and staging share the same client. A network attacker who can intercept traffic (compromised proxy, DNS hijack, malicious Wi-Fi) can present any certificate and read or alter ledger payloads.

The smallest safe fix is to trust the staging CA via `RootCAs` (or a pinned cert) rather than skipping verification. If a temporary skip is unavoidable, it must be behind an explicit non-production flag that defaults to verifying, and must not ship on the production path.

**Recommendation:** request-changes

verification.reason: NewClient() now sets tls.Config{InsecureSkipVerify: true} with no env/build gate; base only used a plain http.Client (default verify). Any caller inherits MITM exposure in all environments.
